title: Public Health Microbiology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L Public Health Microbiology curriculum: modes of disease transmission, water and food sanitary microbiology, indicator organisms and water quality testing, vector-borne and zoonotic diseases, vaccination principles, nosocomial infections, and disinfection/sterilisation practice in public health.

questions.question: Epidemiology is best defined as the study of:
options: The structure and function of individual microbial cells
The distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in populations, and the application of this to disease control
The classification of microorganisms into taxonomic groups
questions.correct_answer: The distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in populations, and the application of this to disease control
questions.explanation: Epidemiology studies how and why disease occurs across populations (person, place, time) so that findings can be applied to prevent and control health problems.

questions.question: A disease that is constantly present at a low, predictable level in a given geographic area is described as:
questions.correct_answer: Endemic
questions.explanation: An endemic disease persists at a baseline, relatively stable level within a specific population or region, as opposed to epidemics (sudden increases) or pandemics (global spread).

questions.question: Herd immunity refers to:
options: Immunity present only in livestock, not humans
Indirect protection from infection conferred on susceptible individuals when a sufficiently large proportion of a population is immune
The innate immune response of a single individual
Immunity that develops only after natural infection, never after vaccination
questions.correct_answer: Indirect protection from infection conferred on susceptible individuals when a sufficiently large proportion of a population is immune
questions.explanation: When enough of a population is immune (through vaccination or prior infection), transmission chains are broken, indirectly protecting susceptible individuals who are not themselves immune.

questions.question: Which route of transmission is responsible for spreading both cholera and typhoid fever?
questions.correct_answer: Faecal-oral route
questions.explanation: Both Vibrio cholerae and Salmonella Typhi are shed in the faeces of infected persons and transmitted when contaminated water or food is ingested — the classic faecal-oral route.

questions.question: The severe watery diarrhoea ('rice-water stool') of cholera is caused mainly by cholera toxin acting to:
options: Increase intracellular cyclic AMP in intestinal epithelial cells, driving massive chloride and water secretion into the gut lumen
Directly invade the bloodstream causing septicaemia
questions.correct_answer: Increase intracellular cyclic AMP in intestinal epithelial cells, driving massive chloride and water secretion into the gut lumen
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates a G protein, permanently activating adenylate cyclase; the resulting rise in cAMP opens chloride channels, causing massive secretion of electrolytes and water into the intestinal lumen.

questions.question: Salmonella Typhi, the causative agent of typhoid fever, is unusual among Salmonella serovars in that it:
options: Is host-adapted to humans (no significant animal reservoir) and can cause a systemic, invasive illness with prolonged bacteraemia
questions.correct_answer: Is host-adapted to humans (no significant animal reservoir) and can cause a systemic, invasive illness with prolonged bacteraemia
questions.explanation: Unlike most non-typhoidal Salmonella serovars, S. Typhi is essentially restricted to human hosts and, rather than causing self-limited gastroenteritis, invades the bloodstream and reticuloendothelial system to cause typhoid fever.

questions.question: In water quality testing, Escherichia coli is the preferred indicator organism for recent faecal contamination mainly because it:
options: Is abundant in human and animal faeces, easily detected, and its presence signals that faecal contamination (and possibly enteric pathogens) may be present
Is more resistant to chlorine than any known pathogen
questions.correct_answer: Is abundant in human and animal faeces, easily detected, and its presence signals that faecal contamination (and possibly enteric pathogens) may be present
questions.explanation: E. coli is consistently and abundantly present in the gut and faeces of warm-blooded animals, is readily cultured and identified, and its detection in water is a practical proxy for the possible presence of harder-to-detect enteric pathogens.

questions.question: The Most Probable Number (MPN) method used in water analysis estimates:
options: The exact number of viable bacteria in a sample
A statistically derived estimate of coliform (or other target organism) density based on the pattern of positive and negative results in serial dilution tubes
The molecular weight of bacterial toxins
The pH of the water sample
questions.correct_answer: A statistically derived estimate of coliform (or other target organism) density based on the pattern of positive and negative results in serial dilution tubes
questions.explanation: The MPN technique uses replicate tubes of serially diluted sample and statistical tables to estimate the most probable density of viable organisms, commonly used for coliform enumeration in water.

questions.question: The membrane filtration technique for water analysis works by:
options: Passing a known volume of water through a fine filter that retains bacteria, then incubating the filter on selective/differential medium to count resulting colonies
Boiling the water sample to kill all organisms before counting
Adding chlorine and measuring residual chlorine only
Centrifuging the sample and weighing the pellet
questions.correct_answer: Passing a known volume of water through a fine filter that retains bacteria, then incubating the filter on selective/differential medium to count resulting colonies
questions.explanation: In membrane filtration, a measured water volume is filtered through a membrane of defined pore size (typically 0.45 µm) that traps bacteria; the membrane is then placed on selective medium and colonies counted directly, giving colony counts per volume filtered.

questions.question: According to standard drinking water quality guidelines, the acceptable coliform count in a 100 mL sample of treated potable water should be:
questions.correct_answer: Zero coliforms detectable
questions.explanation: Safe drinking water standards require that no coliform organisms (including E. coli) be detectable in a 100 mL sample, reflecting the goal of essentially faecal-contamination-free water.

questions.question: Chlorination disinfects drinking water primarily by:
options: Oxidising and damaging microbial cell membranes, enzymes, and nucleic acids, thereby inactivating pathogens
Raising the water's pH to alkaline levels that kill bacteria
questions.correct_answer: Oxidising and damaging microbial cell membranes, enzymes, and nucleic acids, thereby inactivating pathogens
questions.explanation: Chlorine and its hydrolysis product hypochlorous acid are strong oxidising agents that disrupt microbial cell membranes and denature enzymes and nucleic acids, inactivating bacteria, many viruses, and some protozoa.

questions.question: Pasteurisation of milk is designed to:
options: Sterilise the milk completely, killing all microorganisms including spores
Kill pathogenic vegetative organisms (e.g. Mycobacterium bovis, Salmonella, Listeria) and reduce spoilage organisms using controlled heat, without sterilising the product
Add preservatives to extend shelf life indefinitely
Remove all fat-soluble vitamins from milk
questions.correct_answer: Kill pathogenic vegetative organisms (e.g. Mycobacterium bovis, Salmonella, Listeria) and reduce spoilage organisms using controlled heat, without sterilising the product
questions.explanation: Pasteurisation uses a time-temperature combination sufficient to destroy vegetative pathogens and most spoilage organisms while preserving the milk's quality; bacterial endospores and some heat-resistant organisms can survive, so pasteurised milk is not sterile.

questions.question: A zoonotic disease is one that:
options: Is naturally transmissible between vertebrate animals and humans
Can only be transmitted from human to human
questions.correct_answer: Is naturally transmissible between vertebrate animals and humans
questions.explanation: Zoonoses are infections or infectious diseases that are naturally transmitted between vertebrate animals and humans, either directly or via vectors, food, or the environment.

questions.question: Anthrax, a zoonotic disease of major public health concern especially among livestock handlers, is caused by:
questions.correct_answer: Bacillus anthracis
questions.explanation: Bacillus anthracis, a spore-forming Gram-positive rod, causes anthrax, a zoonosis primarily of herbivores that can be transmitted to humans through contact with infected animals or contaminated animal products.

questions.question: Brucellosis, a zoonosis often associated with consumption of unpasteurised dairy products or contact with infected livestock, is caused by species of the genus:
questions.correct_answer: Brucella
questions.explanation: Brucella species (e.g. B. abortus in cattle, B. melitensis in goats) cause brucellosis, transmitted to humans via unpasteurised dairy products or direct contact with infected animals or their tissues.

questions.question: Rabies, an almost invariably fatal zoonotic viral encephalitis, is most commonly transmitted to humans by:
options: The bite or scratch of an infected mammal (commonly dogs), introducing virus-laden saliva
questions.correct_answer: The bite or scratch of an infected mammal (commonly dogs), introducing virus-laden saliva
questions.explanation: Rabies virus is typically transmitted when infected saliva enters a wound from the bite or scratch of a rabid animal, most often dogs in endemic regions, after which the virus travels along peripheral nerves to the central nervous system.

questions.question: A healthcare-associated (nosocomial) infection is defined as an infection that:
options: The patient had before being admitted to a healthcare facility
Is acquired during the course of receiving care in a hospital or other healthcare setting and was not present or incubating at admission
Can only be caused by viruses
Only affects healthcare workers, never patients
questions.correct_answer: Is acquired during the course of receiving care in a hospital or other healthcare setting and was not present or incubating at admission
questions.explanation: Nosocomial (healthcare-associated) infections are those acquired during hospitalisation or treatment that were neither present nor incubating at the time of admission.

questions.question: Which organism is a leading cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and pseudomembranous colitis in hospitalised patients following broad-spectrum antibiotic use?
questions.correct_answer: Clostridioides difficile
questions.explanation: Disruption of normal gut flora by broad-spectrum antibiotics allows Clostridioides difficile to overgrow and produce toxins A and B, causing antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and, in severe cases, pseudomembranous colitis.

questions.question: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is an important nosocomial pathogen because it:
options: Is resistant to all known antimicrobial agents without exception
Carries the mecA gene, conferring resistance to methicillin and most beta-lactam antibiotics, complicating treatment and infection control
questions.correct_answer: Carries the mecA gene, conferring resistance to methicillin and most beta-lactam antibiotics, complicating treatment and infection control
questions.explanation: MRSA strains carry the mecA gene encoding an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) with low affinity for beta-lactams, conferring resistance to methicillin and related drugs and making these strains difficult to treat and important targets of hospital infection control.

questions.question: A live attenuated vaccine differs from an inactivated (killed) vaccine in that it:
options: Contains a weakened but still-replicating form of the pathogen, generally inducing stronger and longer-lasting immunity but carrying some risk in immunocompromised persons
Never contains any part of the actual pathogen
Is always safer for immunocompromised individuals than inactivated vaccines
questions.correct_answer: Contains a weakened but still-replicating form of the pathogen, generally inducing stronger and longer-lasting immunity but carrying some risk in immunocompromised persons
questions.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines use a weakened pathogen that can still replicate to a limited extent, closely mimicking natural infection and typically producing robust, durable immunity, but they pose a theoretical risk of causing disease in immunocompromised individuals, unlike inactivated vaccines.

questions.question: Tetanus and diphtheria vaccines are examples of:
options: Toxoid vaccines, using chemically or heat-inactivated bacterial exotoxins to induce antitoxin immunity
questions.correct_answer: Toxoid vaccines, using chemically or heat-inactivated bacterial exotoxins to induce antitoxin immunity
questions.explanation: Because tetanus and diphtheria disease is caused mainly by potent exotoxins, their vaccines use toxoids (inactivated but still immunogenic toxin) to stimulate protective antitoxin antibodies.

questions.question: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is transmitted between people mainly via:
options: Airborne droplet nuclei expelled by coughing, which can remain suspended and be inhaled by others
questions.correct_answer: Airborne droplet nuclei expelled by coughing, which can remain suspended and be inhaled by others
questions.explanation: Pulmonary tuberculosis spreads chiefly through inhalation of small airborne droplet nuclei containing M. tuberculosis, expelled when an infectious person coughs, sneezes, or speaks.

questions.question: Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Treponema pallidum are both classified as agents of:
questions.correct_answer: Sexually transmitted infection
questions.explanation: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonorrhoea) and Treponema pallidum (syphilis) are both transmitted primarily through sexual contact and are classic bacterial sexually transmitted infections of public health importance.

questions.question: Congenital syphilis, in which Treponema pallidum is transmitted from an infected mother to her fetus, illustrates which mode of transmission?
questions.correct_answer: Vertical (mother-to-child) transmission
questions.explanation: Vertical transmission refers to transfer of an infectious agent from mother to offspring, as occurs when Treponema pallidum crosses the placenta and causes congenital syphilis in the fetus/newborn.

questions.question: An asymptomatic individual who harbours and can transmit a pathogen without showing signs of illness is called a:
questions.correct_answer: Carrier
questions.explanation: A carrier is a person (or animal) who is colonised by a pathogen and can transmit it to others while showing no overt signs or symptoms of disease, complicating outbreak control since carriers are not easily identified clinically.

questions.question: In infection control terminology, an organism, object, or surface that is not itself alive but can passively transfer infectious agents (e.g. a doorknob or shared utensil) is called a:
questions.correct_answer: Fomite
questions.explanation: A fomite is any inanimate object or surface that can become contaminated with pathogens and serve as a means of passive transmission to a new host.

questions.question: Passive disease surveillance, as commonly used in routine public health monitoring, refers to a system in which:
options: Public health officials actively visit every household to search for cases
Healthcare facilities and providers routinely report notifiable diseases to health authorities without the authorities actively seeking out each case
Only laboratory-confirmed outbreaks are ever recorded
Surveillance data are collected only during declared epidemics
questions.correct_answer: Healthcare facilities and providers routinely report notifiable diseases to health authorities without the authorities actively seeking out each case
questions.explanation: Passive surveillance relies on routine reporting of cases by clinicians, laboratories, and health facilities to public health authorities, in contrast to active surveillance, where health workers proactively seek out cases.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of vector-borne disease transmission relevant to public health microbiology in Nigeria?
options: Transmission of Yersinia pestis (plague) via flea bites
Transmission of Vibrio cholerae via contaminated water
Transmission of Mycobacterium tuberculosis via airborne droplets
Transmission of Treponema pallidum via sexual contact
questions.correct_answer: Transmission of Yersinia pestis (plague) via flea bites
questions.explanation: Plague is a classic vector-borne zoonosis in which Yersinia pestis is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected fleas that have fed on infected rodents, distinguishing it from the water-, air-, and contact-borne examples listed.

questions.question: Autoclaving, used in public health facilities to sterilise reusable medical instruments and laboratory waste, achieves sterilisation by:
options: Exposing items to ultraviolet light for several hours
Using saturated steam under pressure (typically 121°C at 15 psi for 15–20 minutes) to kill all microorganisms including bacterial endospores
questions.correct_answer: Using saturated steam under pressure (typically 121°C at 15 psi for 15–20 minutes) to kill all microorganisms including bacterial endospores
questions.explanation: Autoclaving uses pressurised saturated steam, commonly at 121°C for 15–20 minutes, to achieve sterilisation, reliably killing even highly resistant bacterial endospores, unlike chemical disinfection or UV alone.

questions.question: An outbreak in which many people who attended a single event become ill shortly afterward, with no evidence of further person-to-person spread, is characteristic of which type of epidemic pattern?
questions.correct_answer: Common-source (point-source) epidemic
questions.explanation: A common-source epidemic occurs when a group of people are exposed to the same contaminated source (e.g. food at an event) over a short period, producing a sharp, single-peaked epidemic curve without evidence of secondary person-to-person spread.

questions.question: Onchocerciasis (river blindness) in West Africa is transmitted by the bite of infected:
questions.correct_answer: Simulium blackflies
questions.explanation: Onchocerca volvulus, the causative parasite of river blindness, is transmitted by blackflies of the genus Simulium, which breed in fast-flowing rivers, giving the disease its common name.
